**Concept and theory**

Dodd-Frank followed the Madoff fraud and the GFC, both of which renewed scrutiny of hedge funds. Its Title IV, the Private Fund Investment Advisers Registration Act, works on the manager, not the fund vehicle:

- it eliminates the private adviser exemption from the Advisers Act, so the former 15 threshold is no longer relevant and hedge fund managers must register with the SEC;
- it requires hedge funds to submit reports to both the SEC and the FSOC, so regulators can monitor AUM, leverage, counterparty exposures and investment strategies;
- it introduces Form PF (annual from \$150 million AUM, quarterly above \$1.5 billion).

Schweser gives a cluster of facts that, together, made Friehling & Horowitz an implausible auditor for a \$17 billion manager: three people in total; a 550-square-foot office; one partner, Jerome Horowitz, in his late 70s and largely inactive; David Friehling the only practising accountant; and a declaration to the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) that the firm had no auditing clients.
